secretAnswer: Virga is rain or snow that falls from a cloud but disappears before reaching the ground.
supportingFacts: Dry air below the cloud makes the falling water disappear into the air.
It can look like thin tails hanging from a cloud.
revealExplanation: The disappearing water cools the air around it.

sources.title: NOAA National Weather Service: Owlie's Weird Weather

secretAnswer: A snow roller is a roll of snow formed naturally by wind or by rolling downhill.
supportingFacts: The snow must be sticky enough to hold together.
Strong wind can break the roll apart.
revealExplanation: Some rollers have a hollow middle and look like doughnuts.

sources.title: NOAA National Weather Service: Owlie's Weird Weather

secretAnswer: Hair ice is a mass of very thin ice threads that grows on dead wood with help from a fungus.
supportingFacts: It can form on cold, damp nights.
Chemicals from the fungus help keep the ice in thin strands.
revealExplanation: It often melts in the morning.

sources.title: NOAA National Weather Service: Owlie's Weird Weather

secretAnswer: A lenticular cloud is a lens-shaped cloud formed in waves of air, often behind mountains.
supportingFacts: Moist air rises in a standing wave and forms the cloud.
Its shape can look like a flying saucer.
revealExplanation: The air nearby can be rough for aircraft.

secretAnswer: A nacreous cloud is a very high cloud that shines with pearl-like colors near sunrise or sunset.
supportingFacts: It forms in the lower stratosphere over polar regions.
Its small ice particles scatter light.
revealExplanation: Sunlight can still reach it when the sun is below the horizon.

secretAnswer: A noctilucent cloud is a very high cloud of ice crystals that can still shine after sunset.
supportingFacts: It is in the mesosphere, above ordinary clouds.
Its great height lets it keep reflecting sunlight.
revealExplanation: These clouds are too high to change weather on the ground.

secretAnswer: Mammatus are rounded, pouch-like shapes hanging from the underside of a cloud.
supportingFacts: They often appear below a large thunderstorm cloud.
They can also appear on other types of cloud.
revealExplanation: Their name comes from a Latin word for an udder or breast.

secretAnswer: A Brocken spectre is a person's shadow on mist or cloud that appears like a huge distant figure.
supportingFacts: The sun is behind the person.
People often see it from mountain tops.
revealExplanation: It was named after a mountain in Germany.

secretAnswer: A parhelion is a bright spot beside the sun caused by sunlight passing through ice crystals.
supportingFacts: The crystals have six sides.
These spots are also called sun dogs.
revealExplanation: They can appear with a ring of light around the sun.

secretAnswer: A circumzenithal arc is a colored arc in the sky that looks like an upside-down rainbow.
supportingFacts: Sunlight passes through flat ice crystals.
Lower clouds can hide the arc.
revealExplanation: The crystals bend light rather than raindrops making a rainbow.

secretAnswer: A fogbow is a pale, often almost white bow of light made by tiny water drops in fog or mist.
supportingFacts: Its water drops are smaller than raindrops.
It is wider than a typical rainbow.
revealExplanation: The tiny drops spread the colors so they are hard to see.

secretAnswer: A moonbow is a rainbow made by moonlight instead of sunlight.
supportingFacts: It often looks white to our eyes because its light is weak.
A nearly full, low moon and water drops can make one possible.
revealExplanation: A long-exposure photo can show its faint colors.

secretAnswer: Alexander's band is the darker area between the two bows of a double rainbow.
supportingFacts: The outer rainbow is fainter than the inner one.
The outer bow's colors run in the opposite order.
revealExplanation: Less rainbow light reaches your eyes from the area between the bows.

secretAnswer: Tafoni are small, rounded holes in a rock surface that can look like a honeycomb.
supportingFacts: Groups of holes can make the rock look like a sponge.
They often occur in dry or partly dry areas.
revealExplanation: At Arches, water helps weaken the material holding sandstone together.

secretAnswer: A fulgurite is glass formed when lightning melts sand in the ground.
supportingFacts: In sand dunes, it can form dark glass tubes.
The name comes from the Latin word for lightning.
revealExplanation: The tubes preserve part of the path of a lightning strike through sand.

secretAnswer: A fallstreak hole is a large round or oval gap that forms when ice grows and falls out of a cloud.
supportingFacts: The cloud can contain liquid drops colder than freezing.
An aircraft passing through can help start the freezing.
revealExplanation: The gap can grow as nearby drops freeze and fall.

secretAnswer: Desert varnish is a thin natural coating that gives exposed rocks dark or reddish colors.
supportingFacts: It may contain clay and iron or manganese oxides.
Its material is different from the rock beneath it.
revealExplanation: People have made rock carvings by cutting through the dark surface to reveal lighter rock.

secretAnswer: Pillow lava is rounded lumps of rock formed when lava cools quickly in water.
supportingFacts: The outside cools into a glassy skin.
Hot lava inside can keep making the lump larger.
revealExplanation: The lumps can pile up in thick stacks.

secretAnswer: A yardang is a ridge of rock shaped by wind wearing away the surrounding material.
supportingFacts: Wind can carry away loose sand grains from the rock.
NASA has photographed yardangs on Mars.
revealExplanation: Their shape records the action of rock-wearing winds.

secretAnswer: A helictite is a twisted mineral growth in a cave that can grow in many directions.
supportingFacts: It can grow on cave ceilings or walls.
Water moves through tiny channels inside it.
revealExplanation: Some look like thin branches or antlers rather than straight hanging points.

secretAnswer: Pele's hair is thin strands of volcanic glass made when liquid lava is stretched and cools in air.
supportingFacts: It forms from very fluid lava.
Wind can carry the light strands away from a volcano.
revealExplanation: The strands are fragile and can break into sharp glass pieces.

secretAnswer: Pele's tears are small droplets of volcanic glass made from liquid lava.
supportingFacts: They can occur in a cloud of cooled lava pieces above a lava fountain.
They are droplets, while Pele's hair forms thin strands.
revealExplanation: Very fluid lava can form drops rather than long strings.

sources.title: US Geological Survey: Hawaiian lava fountain and volcanic glass

secretAnswer: Kleptoplasty is when an organism takes the light-catching parts of its food and keeps using them in its own cells.
supportingFacts: Some sea slugs take these parts from algae they eat.
The stolen parts can still use sunlight to provide energy.
revealExplanation: The name's first part comes from a Greek word for thief.

secretAnswer: A witch's broom is a dense bunch of unusually short shoots growing together on a tree or other woody plant.
supportingFacts: Diseases, mites, or mutations can cause it.
Many short shoots can grow after a main growing point dies.
revealExplanation: Some caused by mutations are used to grow dwarf plants.

sources.title: University of Maryland Extension: Witches' Broom on Trees

secretAnswer: Guttation is when pressure in a plant's roots pushes liquid water out at the edges of its leaves.
supportingFacts: It can be seen on lawn grass.
The drops often appear in the morning after little water has evaporated.
revealExplanation: The water comes from inside the plant.

sources.title: Nature Education: Water Uptake and Transport in Vascular Plants

secretAnswer: Countershading is coloring with a dark upper side and a light lower side that helps an animal blend in.
supportingFacts: From above, the dark side can match deep water.
From below, the light side can match the bright surface.
revealExplanation: Tuna, sharks, dolphins, and sea turtles use this form of camouflage.

secretAnswer: Marcescence is when a plant keeps dead leaves attached instead of dropping them at the usual time.
supportingFacts: Oaks and beech trees can keep dead leaves through winter.
New spring growth can push the old leaves off.
revealExplanation: Researchers have several ideas about its benefits, but the reason is not settled.

sources.title: University of Georgia Extension: Trees that hold their leaves

secretAnswer: Plant vivipary is when a seed starts growing while still inside or attached to its parent plant.
supportingFacts: It can happen inside a tomato.
For some mangroves, it is a normal way to develop.
revealExplanation: A mangrove seedling can drop with a long root that sticks into soft wet soil.

secretAnswer: Nyctinasty is the daily movement of some plant leaves as day turns to night.
supportingFacts: Shamrock plants fold their leaves at night and open them in morning light.
Special cells at the leaf base swell or shrink to move it.
revealExplanation: The leaves can look as if they are going to sleep.

sources.title: University of Missouri Extension: Shamrock plants

secretAnswer: Masting is when trees or shrubs produce a huge seed crop in some years and much less in others.
supportingFacts: Their fruits and seeds are an important food for wildlife.
Oaks and beech trees have years with heavy nut crops.
revealExplanation: Weather, species, and genetics all help affect how much seed is produced.

sources.title: University of New Hampshire Extension: Mast
